card.hook: Golden roofs, a slow river and old stone steps, all in one frame. Pashupatinath is one of those places where you'll take the photo and then forget to put your phone away.
card.stand_here: Stand on Arya Ghat, the stone steps on the eastern bank of the Bagmati facing the aarati platform. The temple is about 44 metres to the north-east of that point, so face north-east and look across the river.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the roofs, river and ghats in one frame. Try 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the golden roofs. Zoom 0.5x is fun for the steps and the crowd, but the temple will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the gold roof, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the gold keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon, roughly 3:30 to 5:00 PM, when the light falls on the golden roof. Then stay on for the evening aarati.
card.selfie_here: Our best lead is the Pashupatinath Viewpoint, on the hilltop across the river, where the golden roof is in view. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the roof over your shoulder. We can't promise it's a classic selfie spot, so check the angle on your screen first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by on the eastern bank, facing the back of the temple, so the whole temple fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a living place of worship, so keep your distance from mourners and any cremation, never use flash near the rites, and leave drones at home. Photography isn't allowed inside the main sanctum and non-Hindus can't enter it, so check the official site for current rules. Keep valuables secure in crowds, and note that sadhus may expect a tip of NPR 100 to 300 for photos.
card.challenge: Get the golden roofs on the upper third with the water's edge or the steps in the foreground, and then see if you can catch the river looking calm.
card.good_to_know: Pashupatinath is a Hindu temple to Pashupati, a form of Shiva, and has been part of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage listing since 1979. The main temple is a Newari-style pagoda about 23 metres tall, with gold-covered copper roofs, and it sits among 518 mini-temples. It's recorded as early as 400 CE, and its present form dates from a renovation in 1692.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Arya Ghat, the stone steps on the eastern bank of the Bagmati facing the aarati platform. The temple is about 44 metres to the north-east of that point, so face north-east and look across the river.

card.hook: Giant painted eyes are watching you from the top of this hill, and so are a few monkeys. Swayambhunath is the Monkey Temple, and the eyes on the white dome look out in all four directions.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, on the upper terrace on the northeast/east side of the dome. There's no extra walk once you're there. Turn back to face the valley, with the gold spire and Buddha eyes close in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the dome and spire with some valley behind. Go to 0.5x to fit the terrace, flags and view together, then try 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the Buddha eyes and gold rings.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the Buddha eyes, then drag the brighter/darker slider down a little so the gold and white don't burn out against the sky.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the sun lights the eastern face and before the haze builds. Clear Himalaya views are seasonal, mainly October to February.
card.selfie_here: Head to the main stupa platform, close to the base of the stupa with the strings of prayer flags behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the stupa and fluttering flags fill in behind your shoulder. For softer light, the platform on the northeast side of the dome in early morning is the most flattering backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: The monkeys can bite, so don't touch them and keep food and valuables out of their reach. This is an active place of worship, so look for no-photography signs before shooting inside any shrine and ask before photographing worshippers. Some areas may be closed after earthquake damage, and an entrance fee may apply, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Count the thirteen gold rings above the eyes, then take one shot with the spire lined up perfectly on a vertical gridline.
card.good_to_know: The thirteen gold-plated rings above the eyes stand for the stages before nirvana. The stupa was renovated in May 2010, its first major renovation since 1921, and re-gilded with 20 kg of gold. UNESCO listed the site in 1979.

card.hook: Step through the gate and the Thamel noise just drops away, like someone found the volume knob. Then you hit the central pond, and the pavilions are sitting there twice: once in real life, once in the water.
card.stand_here: Stand at the central lotus pond in the Garden of Dreams, right where the phone icon is on the map. Turn around to face back toward the pavilions, so the buildings and flower beds line up with their reflection in the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the pavilions and their reflection in one frame. If the buildings get cut off, drop to zoom 0.5x. Try zoom 2x or 5x for close-ups of an urn or a pergola (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower line, so the pavilions fill the top and their reflection fills the bottom.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet, when the water is calm enough to give a proper mirror image. Hold your phone as still as you can and the reflection stays crisp.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Barkha Pavilion and stand in front of it, so the pavilion fills the background behind you. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x if you want more of the building in the shot. The Open Air Theatre also works, with its tiered seating behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Normal photos are fine, but videos need prior approval from management. No photos in the Kaisher Gallery or the garden's office areas. Drones are typically prohibited. Bring a hat and put on sunscreen, and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the pavilion reflection is so good that a friend has to look twice to tell which way up the photo is.
card.good_to_know: The garden was laid out in 1920 as a private garden for Field Marshal Kaiser Sumsher Rana, designed by Kishore Narshingh. After decades of neglect it was restored between 2000 and 2007. About 6,895 square metres remain, with three pavilions, an amphitheatre and several ponds.

card.hook: Picture a cycle rickshaw, a wall of woolly hats and signs stacked three high, all squeezed into one lane. That's Thamel, and it's wonderfully messy.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon near Keshar Mahal Marg, about 390 m east of the subject, and face west. Then walk west into the lanes and stop at a corner or wider junction where you can shoot down a street without blocking it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for street scenes. Switch to 0.5x in the tightest alleys to fit the shopfronts and the signs above them. Use zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for details like goods on display, so you don't block anyone's way.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and use the lane as a guide line, with shopfronts on both sides and a person or rickshaw as your star.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, so you get clearer shots of the lanes. In the evening the signs and shop lights come on and the street gets more colour, but it's busier.
card.selfie_here: Head to Mandala Street and stand with the fairy-lit shopfronts, bookshops and cafés behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the glow in, and keep the lights over your shoulder. For a colourful change, try the Lord Buddha mural wall on Saat Ghumti.
card.rules_and_safety: Vehicles squeeze past pedestrians here and there are no footpaths, so step aside carefully when you pose. Ask before taking close portraits of shopkeepers or vendors.
card.challenge: Pick a lane, hold your phone steady and wait a few seconds until a rickshaw rolls into the gap, then snap.
card.good_to_know: Thamel is Kathmandu's best-known tourist neighbourhood, about 1.4 km north of Durbar Square. The name comes from Tha Bahi, a Newar name. It has been the centre of the visitor trade for over four decades, since the hippie days when artists came to Nepal and stayed for weeks.

card.hook: Picture a square where bead sellers, pilgrims and rickshaws all squeeze past each other, while a big mask of the 'god of the sky' watches over it. That's Indra Chowk, and it's all fair game for your camera roll.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Akash Bhairav Temple side, on the west of the square, and face across the junction. You want the shrine window and its lamplight in front of the old merchant houses.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the temple and the junction together. If the lane feels too tight, drop to 0.5x. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the shrine window and lamps, so you don't have to step into worshippers' space.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest lamp, then slide the picture a little darker so the flames keep their glow.
card.best_time: Dusk is best, especially during Indra Jatra in September when the oil lamps are lit. It gets very crowded then, and the street layout changes, so give yourself extra time.
card.selfie_here: Try the temple steps of Akash Bhairav Temple, looking out over the Indra Chowk junction. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the busy square and old houses behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The lanes here are narrow and share space with vehicles and rickshaws, so keep an eye on your surroundings while you frame your shot. Check local signs too, as photo rules and access to the temple's upper floor may vary.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the shrine window on one third of the frame, and catch a lamp glow, an old house front and one passing rickshaw in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: Indra Chowk is one of the old ceremonial and market squares on Kathmandu's historic trade street. The Akash Bhairav temple is its symbol, and its mask is the 'god of the sky'. During Indra Jatra, the chariots of Kumari, Ganesh and Bhairav are pulled right through the square.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Akash Bhairav Temple side, on the west of the square, and face across the junction. You want the shrine window and its lamplight in front of the old merchant houses.

card.hook: Two painted wooden figures lean out of an upper window, Shiva and Parvati, looking down at the square like neighbours watching the street. Everything below them is busy, so you get a whole day of Kathmandu in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Shiva-Parvati Temple on the western side of the square, and face the first-floor window where the figures lean out. Keep the busy square in front of you so it fills the bottom of your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the window, the figures and the square. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the painted faces and the carved wood. Save zoom 0.5x for a whole-square shot, and keep people and the temple away from the edges of the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the window on one of the upper lines, so the square and its people fill the lower part of the frame.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 7:30 AM. One guide says the square is quieter then and the morning light is better.
card.selfie_here: Climb the broad steps of the Maju Dega temple, the big Shiva temple in the square, and turn your front camera around so the temple is behind you. Try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the square in, with the temple over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: The rooftop terrace of Cafe Soma on Freak Street looks down on the square, so you could stand in the square while someone up there shoots down at you. It's a café, so you'd normally buy something, and it's worth checking it's open first.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't photograph the Kumari herself, and don't take photos inside the Kumari Bahal courtyard or the palace museums. Cameras aren't allowed in the museum buildings, and flash is discouraged inside temples. Look for signs and follow them, as some areas have photo rules.
card.challenge: Take one frame with people in it for scale, then wait for a gap and see if you can get one without. Which one do you like more?
card.good_to_know: This old royal square is also called Hanuman Dhoka or Basantapur Durbar Kshetra, and it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The nine-storey Nautalle Durbar was built by Prithvi Narayan Shah to mark the Unification of Nepal. The earthquake of 25 April 2015 badly damaged the square, and the old wooden Kasthamandap was lost.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Shiva-Parvati Temple on the western side of the square, and face the first-floor window where the figures lean out. Keep the busy square in front of you so it fills the bottom of your shot.

card.hook: Picture a huge white dome with a pair of painted eyes gazing out over it, and a steady stream of pilgrims walking around the bottom. That's Boudhanath, and it all fits in one frame if you climb up a little.
card.stand_here: Head up to the rooftop terrace of Best View Restaurant, inside the Boudhanath complex, and check its name and location on the map first. Face the stupa so the dome fills the view, framed by the buildings around the square.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the framed rooftop view. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the painted eyes and the pilgrims below. Drop to 0.5x if you want the whole dome with the rooftops around it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the dome on one side with the spire reaching up, then tap the white dome and slide it a little darker so the white keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white dome, and people disagree on whether dawn or sunset wins, so take your pick. After dark the stupa is floodlit, so switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the rail.
card.selfie_here: A visitor review names the rooftop of the building facing the temple entrance as the best photo spot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the stupa behind you over your shoulder. Check the dome is actually in the shot before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the open square around the stupa's base, standing at the outer edge of the path so nobody is blocked, while you stand with the dome behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Boudhanath is a place of worship, so ask before photographing monks or people at prayer, and follow any posted rules on flash. The stupa charges an entrance fee, and rooftop access may need a purchase or fee.
card.challenge: Get the painted eyes, a few prayer flags and the pilgrims' circuit into one shot, and see if you can make the eyes look like they're watching you.
card.good_to_know: Boudhanath is the largest spherical stupa in Nepal and one of the largest in the world. The present stupa was most likely built in the 14th century, though local chronicles mention one here as early as the 5th. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, and the square is now ringed by more than 50 monasteries.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to the rooftop terrace of Best View Restaurant, inside the Boudhanath complex, and check its name and location on the map first. Face the stupa so the dome fills the view, framed by the buildings around the square.

card.hook: Here's a nice trick: one spot on the map gives you two photos. A slim white tower against the sky from the ground, then the whole Kathmandu Valley from the glass deck up top.
card.stand_here: Stand right at Dharahara in Sundhara, because the phone icon sits on the tower itself. For the ground shot, face the tower. For the valley, go up to the glass deck and face the east side for the city view.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x at the foot of the tower to fit the whole height in. Up on the deck, zoom 1x covers the main valley view, and zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) picks out distant hills and temple roofs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines on the ground so the tower stands up straight, and tilt your phone up as little as you can.
card.best_time: Early morning is best for mountain views. Late afternoon gives nicer light on the city.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the street-level ground right at the foot of the tower, use the front camera at 0.5x and let the tower rise over your shoulder. Look up and you may get a sky full of blue and purple, since the purple comes from jacaranda trees that only bloom for part of the year.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in the park around the tower to step back to frame the whole tower while you stand near its foot.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are fine, but professional or commercial shoots need a separate paid permit. The ruins are a memorial, so keep any photos there respectful.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole tower, then one close-up of the broken brick of the old base beside it. Can you make them look like two different places?
card.good_to_know: Dharahara was built in the early 1830s as a watchtower and rebuilt after the 2015 earthquake brought most of it down. It's about 72 metres tall, with a bronze mast on top. The new tower was inaugurated in April 2021 and fully opened to the public in September 2024. The observation deck needs an entry ticket, so check the official site before you go.

card.hook: Most palaces hide behind a long drive and a lot of lawn. This one sits right on Durbar Marg, so you can get the whole front from the street, with shops, cafes and a fair bit of traffic around you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Durbar Marg, opposite the main palace gate, at the north end of the avenue. Face the palace so the gate and the wide front facade line up down the length of the road.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the straight-on view of the facade and gate. If the avenue and the full width of the palace won't fit, try zoom 0.5x. Then go to zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tall central tower and the gate details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the gate up with the centre of the frame, so the symmetry does the work for you.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the sun isn't directly overhead, should give softer, more even light on the facade. Earlier in the day the street is likely to be quieter too.
card.selfie_here: If you're allowed into the grounds, the main palace entrance steps are a good spot: use the front camera and keep the palace behind you. The ornate fountains in the landscaped royal gardens are another place visitors pose, so try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the grounds in.
card.ask_someone: If photos are allowed when you arrive, ask a friendly visitor to take your picture while you stand in front of the main palace entrance steps.
card.rules_and_safety: No photos inside the palace buildings, and phones go in the cloakroom lockers at the gate before the metal detector. Sources disagree on whether you can take photos in the grounds, so check the signs when you arrive.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the tall central tower and see if you can get it perfectly centred, with no bus or scooter sneaking into the shot.
card.good_to_know: This was the royal palace of Nepal and opened as a museum in 2008, after the monarchy ended. King Mahendra ordered the building in 1963 and it was finished in 1969. The American architect Benjamin Polk designed it with Nepalese building styles. The name comes from the Narayana temple opposite and a traditional stone water spout east of the main entrance.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Durbar Marg, opposite the main palace gate, at the north end of the avenue. Face the palace so the gate and the wide front facade line up down the length of the road.

card.hook: Kasthamandap is the quiet star of a very noisy square, and the pigeons, vendors and bustle in front of it are what make your photo feel like Kathmandu. Don't just snap the building. Grab the whole scene.
card.stand_here: Stand in Basantapur Durbar Square, on the open ground in front of the pavilion. The pavilion lies to the west of it, about 340 m on foot, so face west across the square.
card.zoom: From here the pavilion looks fairly small, so start at 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring it closer. Switch to 1x when you want the pigeons, vendors and square all in one shot. If you use 0.5x, keep the pavilion away from the edges of the frame, where buildings can look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the roof lines level, then tap the pavilion and drag the brighter/darker slider down a touch if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer in the square, with fewer people walking through your frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps of Taleju Temple, the tallest temple in the square, for a wide look across the whole square. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and tilt it so the roofline sits over your shoulder, but we can't promise the pavilion will fit behind you, so check your screen before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the open square while you stand in front of the pavilion's main facade (the classic angle), and remember the square is tight, so the whole building may not fit.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the pavilion is prohibited. Ask permission before taking close-ups of people, including sadhus and priests. Drones are generally restricted at heritage sites in Kathmandu, including Durbar Square.
card.challenge: Get a few pigeons in the lower third and the pavilion above them, then try a Live Photo to catch the moment they take off.
card.good_to_know: Kasthamandap means "wood-covered shelter", and it served as a public shelter as well as a temple. The original was destroyed in the April 2015 earthquake, so the building you see now is a reconstruction. Digs after the quake found that the oldest parts date to the 7th century CE. Scaffolding may still be up, so check the current state of the building before you plan your shot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Basantapur Durbar Square, on the open ground in front of the pavilion. The pavilion lies to the west of it, about 340 m on foot, so face west across the square.

card.hook: Picture a small white temple floating on a square pond, with Kathmandu traffic honking just behind you. That calm, mirror-like scene is why people stop at Rani Pokhari.
card.stand_here: Stand at Rani Pokhari on the entrance side of the pond, right where the phone icon is on the map. Face the temple on the island in the middle of the water.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the temple and its reflection in one shot. Go to 0.5x if you want the whole pond, the trees and the sky, or 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) to pick out the roof and details across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the temple, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white walls don't blow out, and turn on gridlines to line the temple up on the centre line.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or sunset, when the reflection is strongest. Wait for a moment when the water is still, because ripples break the mirror.
card.selfie_here: Try the northern gate of Rani Pokhari at sunset, using the front camera at 0.5x with the pond over your shoulder. It's described as a great view of the pond rather than a proven selfie spot, so check how it looks when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: The pond is fenced and the temple is open only on certain festival days, so photograph it from outside. Drones are generally restricted here, so assume they're not allowed. Please ask before taking close-up photos of people.
card.challenge: Take a quick burst or Live Photo and find the one frame where the temple and its reflection look like twins.
card.good_to_know: King Pratap Malla had the pond built in 1670 for his queen, who was grieving after their son was killed by an elephant. It measures about 180 m by 140 m. The temple was rebuilt after the 2015 earthquake, finished in October 2020, and is now in the older Shikhara style. Look for the Ghanta Ghar clock tower across the road to the east and a stone elephant statue on the southern bank.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Rani Pokhari on the entrance side of the pond, right where the phone icon is on the map. Face the temple on the island in the middle of the water.

card.hook: Two stone lions, one very grand white palace, and a road that lets you fit the lot into a single frame. Not bad for a Kathmandu photo stop.
card.stand_here: Stand on Singha Durbar Marg, about 1.9 km south of the marker, on the road opposite the main gate with the lion statues. Face the gate so the palace front is right behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close, so the gate and the whole palace front fit in. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the lions and façade details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white façade, then slide it a touch darker so the white keeps its detail instead of going flat.
card.best_time: Early morning and late afternoon, according to a visitor guide.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the main gate next to the lion statues, with the façade behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if the palace won't fit, and keep the lions and the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Singha Durbar Marg facing the main gate and façade, while you pose by the lion statues so they can shoot the grand front straight on.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay outside the walls. Photography inside the complex and of government activity is prohibited, so keep your shots to the gate, the lions and the façade, and don't point your phone at guards or officials. The site was damaged in 2025, so check locally or on an official site that access around it is open before you go.
card.challenge: Get a portrait of one lion with the palace softly blurred behind it, and give it your best 'I'm the guard here' face.
card.good_to_know: Chandra Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana built Singha Durbar, the 'Lion's Palace', in 1908. It started as a small private home, grew during construction, and was soon sold to the Government of Nepal as the Prime Minister's residence. Its mix of Palladian, Neoclassical and Baroque styles gives the white façade its grand look, and today it houses government offices, including the Federal Parliament. It has survived a fire in 1973, serious damage in the 2015 earthquake and another fire during the September 2025 protests, so what you see now may differ from older pictures.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Singha Durbar Marg, about 1.9 km south of the marker, on the road opposite the main gate with the lion statues. Face the gate so the palace front is right behind it.

card.hook: Six streets crash into one square here, and every one seems to bring a spice pile, a flower seller or a tiny shrine with it. Your phone will be busy.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of Asan Tol, between the potted trees by the small Narayan shrine, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Turn slowly and pick the view where the market lanes meet in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole junction, stalls and shrines into one frame. Switch to 1x for vendors and people, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for spices, flower sellers or the Annapurna temple roofs without pushing into the crowd.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the building edges straight, then tap a bright part of the scene and slide to darker so the shrine roofs and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. The light is softer and the square is quieter, so your wide shot has room to breathe.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x so you and the busy square both fit. Hold the phone slightly above eye level and keep the market, a shrine or a temple roof over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On Ason Road, about 200 m walking down from Ason Chowk with the Annapurna Temple on your left, the temple is visible, so it's a good stretch to ask a passer-by to take your picture.
card.rules_and_safety: The shrines and courtyards around the square are places of worship, so be respectful. Ask vendors and passers-by before taking close-up portraits.
card.challenge: Find the stone fish called Nyālon at the centre and get it into a frame with a pile of spices or a vendor behind it.
card.good_to_know: Asan sits on one of the two legendary India-Tibet trade routes through Kathmandu, which is why it has been a main marketplace since ancient times. The Annapurna Ajimā temple, dedicated to the goddess of abundant grain, presides over the square. The Ganesh temple on the northern side had its tile roofs replaced in 1928.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of Asan Tol, between the potted trees by the small Narayan shrine, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Turn slowly and pick the view where the market lanes meet in front of you.

card.hook: Seen from above, Maitighar Mandala is a neat set of rings. From the pavement it's a big, bold painted disc with a flag in the middle, sitting calmly in the middle of Kathmandu's traffic noise.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pedestrian walkway around the traffic island at Maitighar Mandala, where the phone icon is. Face the flag at the centre, keep well back from the kerb, and never step into the road.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the whole circle and the greenery around it. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the petals, vajras and the flag.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the flag in the centre and hold your phone level so the circles don't look lopsided.
card.best_time: Evening or night is the best time, when the coloured lights are on. For night shots, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows against your body to keep still. Daytime works too if you want clear, bright colours.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement beside the traffic island at the Maitighar Mandala junction, with your back to the mandala so the island fills the frame behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the mandala over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement and don't step onto the roadway or island for a shot. The recessed mandala is hard to see from the road and the traffic is heavy, so keep your phone away from the road edge, use your wrist strap if you have one, and expect gatherings to change access on some days.
card.challenge: Can you find a close-up of a lotus petal and a vajra, and still get the flag in a straight, level shot of the whole circle?
card.good_to_know: The mandala was built in 2001 for the 11th SAARC summit and has been restored since. The outer ring has 32 vajras, the next has 16 lotus petals and the inner ring has 32 garlands. Black stands for anger, orange for love and blue for compassion, and the four corners carry Ashtamangal symbols.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pedestrian walkway around the traffic island at Maitighar Mandala, where the phone icon is. Face the flag at the centre, keep well back from the kerb, and never step into the road.

card.hook: Two white lions sit guard at the door, and above them a wall of dark carved timber glows against warm red brick. It's one of those spots where the building does the showing off for you.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, on the square outside the entrance of Kumari Ghar, near the two white lion statues in the southern part of Basantapur Durbar Square. Face the building so all three storeys rise in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole facade. If the square is busy or you can't step back far enough, tap 0.5x to fit all three storeys in. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the carved windows and balconies.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's straight vertical edges with them, so the facade doesn't lean, then tap the carved woodwork and drag a little darker to keep the red brick rich.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the sunlight picks out the carved woodwork, according to one guide. Give yourself a few minutes for the details.
card.selfie_here: Try the entrance steps between the two white stone lions: front camera, lions beside you, brick facade and carved details over your shoulder (0.5x on the front camera fits more in). If the inner courtyard is open for photos that day, the carved balconies behind you make a good second spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the open paving in front of the white Gaddi Baithak and shoot back across the square while you stand by the lions at the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Never photograph the Kumari herself. If she appears at a window, put your phone away. Check for signs on site (especially about the courtyard), stay in public areas and don't block any ceremonial route. Watch your step: the paving is uneven and there can be construction or changing access around restored monuments.
card.challenge: Can you get both lions low in the frame and every carved window above them, with the building standing perfectly straight?
card.good_to_know: Kumari Ghar is a three-storey red-brick building, and its carved wooden windows and balconies are a great example of Newar architecture. It's a religious residence, so treat it with care. The entrance area is also called Kumari Chowk.

card.hook: A dark, six-armed figure stands over someone he's trampled, and he's right in front of an old palace wall. You couldn't ask for a more dramatic backdrop.
card.stand_here: Walk about 300 m west to reach the statue, on the northwest side of Kathmandu Durbar Square in front of the Hanuman Dhoka palace. Face the statue so the palace fills the space behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the statue and the palace together. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the face, the raised arms and the figure underneath. Use zoom 0.5x only if you're very close, and keep the statue away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the statue on one of the vertical lines, then tap the statue and make the picture a little darker so the black stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: People often pray at the statue, so a clear front-on shot may take some patience. Wait for a gap rather than asking anyone to move.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and keep the statue over your shoulder, with the palace wall behind it. Zoom 0.5x gives you more of the scene if there's room, but keep your face away from the edges. Leave a clear path for people who've come to pray.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so dress respectfully and ask before photographing local people. Photos of the Living Goddess Kumari are forbidden, and the Kumari Ghar building is off-limits for photos. Flash is discouraged inside temples.
card.challenge: Take three shots: one wide with the palace, one close on the face, and one of the arms reaching up. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Kaal Bhairav is a Hindu shrine in Kathmandu Durbar Square, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Legend says the figure was found in a paddy field and later moved to the square by King Pratap Malla. It's believed to be carved from a single stone.

card.hook: Most people shoot Taleju Temple from the busy courtyard floor, elbow to elbow with everyone else. Climb a few steps and you get a calmer, slightly raised view instead.
card.stand_here: Head for the steps at Hanuman Dhoka in Kathmandu Durbar Square, on the side opposite the courtyard. Climb them, then turn back towards the temple, which lies to the north-east. Check the exact steps when you get there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the temple and a bit of the square. Go to 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the stacked roofs and carvings. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the temple look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the temple's upright edges up with the sides of the screen, then tap the temple walls and drag the slider a little darker if the sky is bright so the roofs don't wash out.
card.best_time: Close to sunset or on a sunny morning. Take a few frames and compare them, because the light changes the look a lot.
card.selfie_here: We don't have a proven selfie spot here, so keep it simple. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so more of the temple fits, and hold your phone low and tilted up with the temple over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to shoot from the southeast corner of the outer courtyard, where the whole temple height fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the outside are fine, but the main temple is closed to the public and you can't take photos inside. Tickets may be needed for the square, and the temple has been reported as under renovation, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Fill the top of your frame with roofs and the bottom with steps, then take three versions and pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Taleju Temple is dedicated to Taleju Bhawani, the royal patron goddess of the Malla dynasty. Mahendra Malla built it in 1564, and it's part of Kathmandu Durbar Square, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The temple opens only once a year, at Dashain.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the steps at Hanuman Dhoka in Kathmandu Durbar Square, on the side opposite the courtyard. Climb them, then turn back towards the temple, which lies to the north-east. Check the exact steps when you get there.

card.hook: Big Ben has a cousin in Kathmandu, and it's hanging out behind a pond. Ghanta Ghar is tall, plain and easy to spot against the sky, which makes it a friendly subject.
card.stand_here: Head to Rani Pokhari and stand on the pond's western edge, then face east across the water toward the tower. Move a step or two until the tower sits clearly behind the water.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the tower, the pond, and the temple and trees on either side. Want the tower bigger? Tap 2x or higher, depending on your phone. Use 0.5x only if you're tight against the water's edge, but the tower will look smaller and its edges may bend.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then tap the tower and slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. In April and May the jacaranda blossom around Tundikhel and Ghanta Ghar adds colour.
card.selfie_here: Try Durbar Marg, at the tower end of the road toward Ratna Park, on the road at the tower's base next to Jame Masjid. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the tower over your shoulder. Treat it as a rough area rather than a perfect spot, and note that one reviewer says the tower looks better lit at night.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a busy public area, so check locally for closures or photography restrictions at Rani Pokhari before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead straight with the water in the bottom of your frame and not a single bus in sight. Patience wins this one.
card.good_to_know: Ghanta Ghar is the oldest clock tower in Nepal, and its name simply means "Hour House". It was built under the Rana prime minister Bir Shumsher and modelled on Big Ben in London. The tower you see today was rebuilt on the original site after the earthquake of 1990 BS (1934) brought the first one down.
